prompt: A 5-node Raft cluster tolerates **2 crashed nodes**. A security review asks whether the same 5 nodes could also tolerate 2 nodes that have been compromised and send **different answers to different peers**. What is the right response?

options.text: Yes: any two majorities of 5 share at least one node, so contradictory decisions are still impossible.
options.explanation: Wrong. Overlap protects against crashes because the shared node is honest. With liars, the shared node may be one of the compromised ones, telling each quorum whatever it wants to hear.

options.text: No: it needs a Byzantine fault-tolerant protocol whose quorums always share at least one honest node, which takes at least 7 nodes for 2 liars.
options.explanation: Correct. In the standard unsigned Byzantine quorum model, 3 × 2 + 1 = 7 nodes with quorums of 5 make any two quorums share at least 3 nodes. At most 2 of those can lie, so an honest node is always in both. Raft is not designed for lying nodes at all.

options.text: Yes, as long as every node checksums its log entries.
options.explanation: Wrong. Checksums detect accidental corruption on disk. A compromised node can compute valid checksums for false data, so they do not stop deliberate lies.

options.text: No, but adding a sixth node fixes it.
options.explanation: Wrong. Even cluster sizes add no tolerance for majority quorums, and six nodes still let two quorums overlap only in nodes that could all be liars. The standard model needs three times the faults plus one.

workedExample:
Ask what the overlap between two quorums has to guarantee.

1. **Crash faults:** a crashed node says nothing, so any node in both quorums tells the truth. With 5 nodes, two majorities of 3 always share at least one node, which is enough. That is why 5 nodes survive 2 crashes.
2. **Byzantine faults:** a liar can tell quorum A "yes" and quorum B "no". If the only shared node is a liar, the two quorums can decide opposite things. So the overlap must contain more nodes than there are liars.
3. With 7 nodes and quorums of 5, any two quorums share at least 3 nodes. At most 2 lie, so at least one honest node is in both.

So the review needs a Byzantine fault-tolerant protocol (PBFT-style) with at least 7 nodes, not just more Raft nodes. Most data-centre systems avoid that cost by assuming crash faults only.

prompt: Raft assumes a **crash-recovery** fault model with durable storage. Which of these failures fall **outside** that model, so Raft gives no safety guarantee if they happen? Select all that apply.

options.text: A node reboots after a power cut with its fsynced log intact.
options.explanation: Inside the model. Crash-recovery means exactly this: the node halts, restarts and still has everything it made durable. Raft handles it.

options.text: A node comes back on a fresh VM with an empty disk but the same identity.
options.explanation: Outside the model. This is amnesia: the node has forgotten its vote and its log, so it can vote twice in one term or help elect a leader missing committed entries.

options.text: A disk silently flips bits in a stored log entry.
options.explanation: Outside the model. Silent corruption makes a node report data it never received, which is closer to a Byzantine fault. Systems add checksums to turn it back into a detectable crash.

options.text: A node is paused for 30 seconds by the hypervisor.
options.explanation: Inside the model. A pause looks like a slow or temporarily crashed node. Raft stays safe; the node simply rejoins and learns about any newer term.

options.text: A disk controller acknowledges fsync but loses the write on power failure.
options.explanation: Outside the model. The node believes its vote or log entry is durable when it is not, so after a restart it can contradict what it promised. This is a known cause of real data loss.

workedExample:
Ask of each failure: "does the node behave as a crashed node that restarts with all its durable state?"

| Failure | Behaves like |
|---|---|
| Reboot, disk intact | crash-recovery |
| Fresh disk, same id | amnesia |
| Bit flip | arbitrary (Byzantine-ish) |
| 30 s pause | slow node |
| Lying fsync | amnesia |

Only the first and fourth fit the model. The lesson: the fault model is a contract with your hardware and operations. If you replace a node, give it a **new identity** and add it through a membership change, rather than reusing the old one with an empty disk.
